title: One bolt
heading: From one bolt to a flat T
intro: Before it is a garment, it is a roll of cloth. Watch it unroll, divide into eight pieces and come together again as a flat T.

labels.title: One bolt, one kimono
body: A bolt is about 36–38 cm wide and about 12 m long, and one bolt makes one kimono {7:p.76}.
In the old units: 9 sun 5 bu to 9 sun 8 bu wide, 3 jō or more long. One shaku, about 38 cm, is 10 sun {7:p.80}.

labels.title: Everything follows the width
body: The proportions of every part of a kimono derive from the width of the bolt {8:p.50}.
A sleeve, for example, is as wide as the shoulder, or up to one sun (about 3.8 cm) wider {8:p.49} {7:p.80}.

labels.title: Eight rectangles
body: Two body panels, two sleeves, two okumi, a collar and an over-collar: eight rectangles {7:p.76}.
No pattern is drafted; the cut only divides {7:p.80}. Sleeves and body panels first, the rest split for okumi and collar, as Ōtsuka Sueko put it in 1972 {7:pp.79-80}.

labels.title: The whole bolt is used
body: The bolt is cut and used entire, with nothing left over {7:p.76}.
Becke, quoting Dalby, gives the first mark of a kimono as <q>[A] geometrical use of standard fabric widths sewn with minimal cutting</q> {4:p.10}.

labels.title: Straight seams, sewn by hand
body: Traditionally a kimono is sewn by hand, without large stitches showing on the face {7:p.76}.
The seams have names: the back seam, senui, and the side seams, wakinui {7:p.77}.

labels.title: No darts, no tucks
body: <q>In its unworn form, a kimono has a completely flat surface.</q> {4:p.10}
Becke again: <q>no tucks or darts are added to the fabric which would provide the garment with a three-dimensional shape</q> {4:p.10}.

line.text: Eight rectangles, and not one dart.

cues.show: Watch the cloth before you read anything.
This roll is a tanmono, a bolt. In the old reckoning, one bolt is one kimono.
Its width is settled before any tailor begins. In sixteen thirty-six the shogunate went further, and fixed by law how long and how wide a bolt of silk had to be.
Keep that width in mind. The width of every part that follows derives from it.
Now the cut. There is no paper pattern. The tailor only divides.
Straight cuts give eight pieces. Every strip has a place, and nothing is thrown away.
Then the pieces are joined again, by hand.
The stitches are sewn so that they barely show on the face. Follow the seams: they run straight, because every piece is straight.
There is no dart, and no curve. Hung on its rack, the robe is as flat as the bolt it came from.
And yet it has to close around a person. Come round to the front, and see how.

claims.text: One bolt is about 36-38 cm wide and about 12 m long, and makes one kimono.
claims.quote: １反（幅約 36～38cm・長さ約 12m）という単位で扱い，１反がキモノ１枚分に相当する
claims.scope: Tr.: "handled in units of one tan (width about 36-38 cm, length about 12 m); one tan equals one kimono". Woman's nagagi; the authors citing a tailoring textbook.

claims.text: Old units: 1 shaku = 10 sun = about 38 cm; standard width 9 sun 5 bu to 9 sun 8 bu; a kimono bolt is 3 jō or more.
claims.quote: １尺＝10 寸＝約 38cm，10 尺＝１丈。並幅は９寸５分～９寸８分，着尺１反は３丈以上。
claims.scope: Tr.: "1 shaku = 10 sun = about 38 cm, 10 shaku = 1 jō. Standard width is 9 sun 5 bu to 9 sun 8 bu; one kijaku bolt is 3 jō or more.". Note 7; kujirajaku units. Also gives 1 sun = about 3.8 cm (label 2).

claims.text: In 1636 a shogunal law fixed the length and width of a bolt of silk.
claims.quote: 絹紬1反の長さかねにて3丈4尺,幅 1尺4寸
claims.scope: Tr.: "one bolt of silk or pongee: length 3 jō 4 shaku in kanejaku, width 1 shaku 4 sun". Kan'ei 13 (1636) shogunal law as given by Nishimura; kanejaku units; silk and pongee (cotton had its own width).

claims.text: The width ratios of the parts derive from the bolt width.
claims.quote: キモノの各部の幅の比率は反物の幅に由来する。
claims.scope: Tr.: "the width ratios of the kimono parts derive from the bolt width". Authors' conclusion (doll-kimono study, concluding section).

claims.text: Sleeve width equals the shoulder width or is up to 1 sun wider.
claims.quote: 袖幅は肩幅と同寸から1寸以内の範囲で広くするため，肩幅1に対し袖幅は1～1.1程度
claims.scope: Tr.: "sleeve width is from the same as shoulder width to within 1 sun wider, so about 1-1.1 to shoulder 1". Standard dimensions, woman's kimono.

claims.text: A woman's nagagi is eight rectangles: two body panels, two sleeves, two okumi, a collar and an over-collar.
claims.quote: 左右の前後身頃２枚，袖２枚，衽２枚，衿１枚，掛衿１枚の８枚の長方形によって構成される
claims.scope: Tr.: "composed of eight rectangles: left and right front-back body panels 2, sleeves 2, okumi 2, collar 1, over-collar 1". Basic form of the modern woman's nagagi, as the authors describe it.

claims.text: No pattern is made; cutting only divides the cloth into eight rectangles.
claims.quote: 衣服の形を決め型紙を作る段階が省略され，８枚の長方形に分けるだけの裁断はとても簡素であり
claims.scope: Tr.: "the step of making a pattern is omitted; cutting that only divides into 8 rectangles is very simple". Authors' interpretation, compared with Western dressmaking.

claims.text: Ōtsuka's rule: cut both sleeves and both body panels, then split the remainder for okumi and collar.
claims.quote: 両袖，両身頃を裁ち，残ったものを二つに割っておくみと衿に分ければいいわけで
claims.scope: Tr.: "cut both sleeves and both bodies, then split what remains in two for okumi and collar". Quotation of Ōtsuka Sueko 1972 inside Maruyama et al.

claims.text: The bolt is cut and used entirely, with nothing left over.
claims.quote: 図１のように裁断し，すべて残らず用いて作る。
claims.scope: Tr.: "cut as in Fig. 1 and made using all of it, with nothing left". Standard layout (the paper's Fig. 1).

claims.text: Dalby's first defining trait: standard fabric widths sewn with minimal cutting.
claims.quote: [A] geometrical use of standard fabric widths sewn with minimal cutting

claims.text: Kimono are traditionally sewn by hand, without large stitches on the face, so that the stitches do not stand out.
claims.quote: 縫製は伝統的に手縫いで行われ，表に大きく縫い目を出さず，目立たないような縫い方で仕立てられる
claims.scope: Tr.: "sewing is traditionally by hand, without showing large stitches on the face, sewn so as not to stand out". General.

claims.text: The seams include the side seams (wakinui) and the back seam (senui).
claims.quote: ６）脇縫いをほどく。７）背縫いをほどく。８）袖をほどく。
claims.scope: Tr.: "6) unpick the side seams. 7) unpick the back seam. 8) unpick the sleeves.". Disassembly order for one sample; names the seams.

claims.text: Cutting the cloth in large straight pieces means few seams, and straight ones.
claims.quote: 布を大きく使った直線的な形は，縫う箇所が少なく直線であり
claims.scope: Tr.: "the straight form that uses the cloth in large pieces has few places to sew, and they are straight". Authors' discussion. Added by verifier.

claims.text: Unworn, a kimono has a completely flat surface.
claims.quote: In its unworn form, a kimono has a completely flat surface.

claims.text: No tucks or darts give it a three-dimensional shape.
claims.quote: no tucks or darts are added to the fabric which would provide the garment with a three-dimensional shape

dropped: Exact cutting lengths for each piece of a standard bolt: only diagrams (Maruyama 2017 Fig. 1; 2020 Fig. 3), no figures in text.
The number of cuts: no source counts them, so the narration does not.
